question.leadin: The command "Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" was issued during this battle.
question.text: Name this June 1775 battle in which American forces lost to a British army on the outskirts of Boston. The location of this battle was actually at Breed's Hill, not at its namesake location.
question.clue: That force repelled two attacks before running out of ammunition during this attempt by British troops to break the Siege of Boston.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about famous forts in American history.
swap.text: This fort, located near Lake Champlain in New York, was captured by the Green Mountain Boys led by Ethan Allen in 1775. A popular brand of pencils also shares this name.
swap.clue: This fort's location near Lake Champlain made it useful in monitoring trade routes between New York and Canada.

question.text: Cornwallis' surrender effectively ended this war.
question.clue: In the leadup to this war, the term "virtual representation" described tariffs passed by Charles Townshend.

swap.text: de Gouges' Declaration of the Rights of Woman was a response to the Declaration of the Rights of Man, a 1789 document written in part by this French general, who had spent several years in America fighting for the colonists.
swap.answerHtml: Marquis de Lafayette (accept Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier)
swap.clue: With the Comte de Mirabeau, this man drafted the Declaration of the Rights of Man, which was modeled after the Declaration of Independence.

question.leadin: According to this person, a certain animal is "a little vain and silly" but "would not hesitate to attack a Grenadier of the British Guards."
question.text: Name this person who called the same animal "a true original native of America." This man was also the oldest delegate to the Constitutional Convention.
question.clue: He served on the Committee of Five and indirectly prompted Louis XVI to sign the Edict of Versailles while an ambassador.

swap.leadin: This general's namesake administrative code gave British people higher status in India than native inhabitants.
swap.text: Name this Governor-General of India, who had earlier surrendered to George Washington at Yorktown.
swap.clue: His namesake "Code" is credited with preventing bureaucratic corruption throughout British rule in India, and he later resigned as viceroy of Ireland in protest over Parliament's denial of Catholic rights.

question.text: At Monmouth, this woman is said to have brought water out to the American soldiers, hence her nickname. She took her husband's place at his cannon after he collapsed.
question.answerHtml: Molly Pitcher [accept Mary Ludwig Hays; prompt on partial]
question.clue: This possibly-legendary woman took her husband's place loading cannons at the Battle of Monmouth during the American Revolution. Her nickname comes from her previous role as a water carrier.

swap.leadin: In a letter written to her husband, this person asked the founding fathers to "remember the ladies."
swap.text: Name this woman, the wife of the second President of the United States.
swap.clue: This person wrote another letter asking to "remember the ladies and be more generous and favorable to them than your ancestors."

question.leadin: Name these northern battles of the American Revolution.
question.text: At this creek on the Pennsylvania-Delaware border, the British won a September 1777 battle for access to Philadelphia.
question.clue: General von Knyphausen led the flanking attack that ended this battle, which was followed by a defeat for Anthony Wayne known as the Paoli Massacre.

swap.text: Tarleton was routed after militia led by Daniel Morgan feigned retreat at this 1781 South Carolina battle that allowed Morgan to join up with Nathaniel Greene's forces.
swap.clue: Colonial soldiers in the first two lines of this battle were ordered by Daniel Morgan to fire at British officers before falling back, which made Banastre Tarleton think they were retreating.

question.leadin: A Danielle Allen book presents a reading of this document "in defense of equality."
question.text: Name this document. Allen contrasts this document's use of the phrase "we hold these truths to be self-evident" with the statement "I believe" in the Catholic Credo.
question.clue: It was drafted by the Committee of Five, including Robert Livingston and Roger Sherman.

swap.text: This governor of Virginia's First Lady Dorothea was cousins with Martha Washington. This man, who claimed he "smelt a rat" at the Constitutional Convention, ended a speech with "Give me liberty or give me death!"
swap.clue: The opening of Daniel Webster's "Seventh of March" address resembles this politician's desire to be seen as "not a Virginian, but an American" in an earlier speech.

question.text: The force that put down the Whiskey rebellion was lead by Washington, Hamilton, and this Revolutionary War hero, who was also the father of the leader of the Confederate forces in the Civil War.
question.answerHtml: Henry “Lighthorse Harry” Lee III (prompt on partial, “H Lee” or “Lighthorse Harry” is needed)
question.clue: This Revolutionary War military figure and ninth governor of Virginia whose son would later lead the Confederate forces. He was nicknamed for his prowess as a cavalry officer.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the Russian navy.
swap.text: This American naval officer joined Catherine the Great's navy for a short-lived campaign on the Black Sea.
swap.clue: He obtained a reputation for cruelty after flogging the carpenter Mungo Maxwell and running-through the leader of a mutiny, causing him to change his name after fleeing Tobago in 1773.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the role pine trees played in the colonial US.
question.text: Joseph Reed, who designed the Pine Tree Flag in 1775, represented Philadelphia as part of committees of correspondence created by this politician. James Otis and this politician co-authored the Massachusetts Circular Letter.
question.clue: Another of his major projects was extended by Dabney Carr, and was planned with Joseph Warren.

swap.text: This American lieutenant colonel at Cowpens was legendarily saved from death by an unnamed Black soldier, who shot a charging British cornet. He was the cousin of a later President.

question.leadin: While working for the Culper Ring, Elizabeth Burgin helped save hundreds of people from these places because women were the only people able to visit them.
question.text: Name these places that the British hulked near New York City. A Martyrs' Monument in Fort Greene Park honors more than 11,000 Americans who died in these places during the Revolutionary War.
question.answerHtml: prison ships [prompt on prisons by asking “in what structures?”; prompt on ships by asking “serving what purpose?”]

swap.text: Some scholars believe that this African-born author helped write that petition. Her other political works include the poem "To His Excellency, General Washington."
swap.clue: This early American poet was the first African-American woman to have her writings published. She included poems praising George Whitefield and George Washington in her Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral.

question.leadin: Answer the following about pre-Revolutionary War protests of British duties, FTPE.
question.text: Opposed in the "Letters of a Westchester Farmer" by Samuel Seabury, this organization was created in 1774 by the Continental Congress to ensure the enforcement of non-importation of dutied goods. It was based on a similarly named program started in Virginia in response to the Townshend Acts.
question.clue: Sherman was one of the signatories of this 1774 agreement, which called for a boycott of all British goods.

swap.text: The company which built the large canal of this name in New Jersey owned many of Indiana's canals after the bankruptcy. This is also the surname of a man who chaired the Erie Canal Commission and wrote the preamble to the U.S. Constitution.
swap.answerHtml: Morris [accept Morris Canal or Gouverneur Morris] (The common-link isn’t accidental, as Morris, New Jersey is named for Gouverneur Morris’s family.)
swap.clue: This was the surname of the so-called "Financier of the Revolution" from Pennsylvania and a New Yorker who wrote the Constitution's preamble.
